That sounds wonderful. A small herb garden on a balcony is very doable, and the flavors really do make a difference compared to store-bought herbs. Here’s a practical, easy-to-follow plan to get you started.

What to grow (easy starters)
- Basil: loves sun; thrives in containers.
- Parsley (flat-leaf or-curly): fairly forgiving; likes some sun.
- Chives: easy, little maintenance, good in a bright spot.
- Mint: very easy, but it spreads aggressively—best in its own pot.
- Cilantro: do this one in a cooler time of year or in a spot with some shade in hotter climates; it can bolt in heat.

Container and space basics
- Pots: aim for at least 6–8 inches deep for each herb; 8–12 inches across is nice if you’re growing a couple in one pot.
- Drainage: make sure pots have drainage holes. Use a light, well-draining potting mix (not garden soil). A mix of potting soil with a bit of perlite or compost works well.
- How many pots: you can start with 2–3 pots (one for basil, one for parsley or chives, one for a mint in its own pot). If you have more space, add a small cilantro pot.

Sun and spot choice
- Most herbs love sun. A south- or west-facing balcony that gets at least 4–6 hours of sun is ideal for basil and mint; parsley and chives are a bit more tolerant of partial sun.
- If your balcony is very hot and exposed, give herbs a bit of afternoon shade or pick partial-sun varieties.

Planting (quick start)
- If you’re starting from nursery plants: gently loosen roots and plant at the same depth they were in their pots.
- If you’re starting from seeds: use seed starting mix and follow packet directions. Seedlings will take longer to harvest but can be cheaper.
- Water after planting to settle the soil, then let the top inch dry before watering again.

Care and maintenance
- Watering: check moisture daily in hot weather. Water deeply when the top inch feels dry; ensure excess water can drain away. Don’t let pots sit in a saucer of standing water.
- Fertilizing: use a balanced, water-soluble fertilizer every 3–4 weeks or a light slow-release fertilizer at planting. Don’t over-fertilize.
- Pruning/harvesting:
  - Basil: pinch off the stems just above a pair of leaves to encourage bushier growth. Regular harvesting keeps the plant productive.
  - Parsley: harvest outer stems first, trim as needed, never remove more than about a third of the plant at once.
  - Chives: snip chive blades as needed; they regrow from the base.
  - Mint: harvest leaves from the outer edges; keep it in its own pot to control spreading.
  - Cilantro: harvest leaves early; it doesn’t like being crowded or overly hot in containers (will bolt in heat).

Common issues and quick fixes
- Wilting in heat: may indicate dry soil. Check soil moisture and water deeply.
- Yellow leaves: could be overwatering or nutrient deficiency; adjust watering and consider a light fertilizer.
- Pests: small aphids or whiteflies occasionally. A gentle spray of water or insecticidal soap can help. Regularly check undersides of leaves.
- Powdery mildew: ensure good airflow and avoid overhead watering late in the day.

Simple starter plan (one example)
- Pot 1: Basil (about 8–10 inches wide)
- Pot 2: Parsley and chives together (a 12-inch pot works well)
- Pot 3: Mint (in its own 8–10 inch pot)
- Optional Pot 4: Cilantro in a small 6–8 inch pot if you enjoy it

Getting ready today
- Find sunny space on your balcony; place pots where you’ll remember to water and prune.
- Fill pots with a good potting mix and plant seedings or herbs.
- Water well after planting, then set a simple routine: check moisture daily in warm weather and water when the top inch is dry.

- Whether you’d prefer buying a few starter plants or starting with seeds,
